# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–33 (Updated 2026-10-13, Post-Excerpt Revision)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of ninth year after Waterloo (1830). Chapter 33 spans Tuesday following Fisker's departure (Saturday, 19th April) through Friday of Whitsun week (May). Georgiana Longestaffe departs Caversham for railway station Friday morning.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn, Queen's Gate); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; Sheepstone; Bungay; Sheep's Acre Farm; Sheepstone Birches; Yarlton; Staveton (harbor town); various American locations; Suffolk.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt**: All deceased as previously documented.

## Rebecca's Arc
- Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) receives liberal allowance but declines to see her. Appears very wealthy at Bath and Cheltenham. Strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
- Married at Dike (Ostend); Amelia initiated encounter in "dripping white bonnet and shawl." Only Georgy and Jos present. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (godmother: Lady Jane) than of his History of the Punjaub.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with Felix and Henrietta. Devoted to children, especially Felix. Authored "Criminal Queens"—pandered to bad tastes through fabricated crime. Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. Mr. Alf denies writing reviews himself; when judgment hostile to personal friend, he laments "accident." Lady Carbury disbelieves, correctly suspecting direct orders from Alf. Proposed scheme to Henrietta: if she married Roger, Felix could inherit his name, title, property. Felix consented to remain at Manor House. At Monday Caversham dinner, sat with Melmotte; found him "heavy on her hands." He stated Felix "don't trouble me much, and I don't trouble him much" regarding directorship. Eager that Felix formally propose to Marie's father; urged him not to delay, warning "don't put it off; you don't know how many slips there may be between the cup and the lip." Felix refused, claiming awkwardness.

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful as star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Became Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Miles Grendall undertook to pay Vossner £450 at three months' end; Vossner produced £322 10s. in notes and gold. Has been in Grosvenor Square since return from Carbury; seen Madame Melmotte and Marie together but engagement not discussed. Madame Melmotte called Miss Longestaffe "fatigante"; Marie declared intention to like Longestaffe very much. **Sunday, 26th April (present scene): Felix knocked at Grosvenor Square door intending to ask for Melmotte but lost courage and was shown to drawing-room where he found Madame Melmotte, Marie, Georgiana Longestaffe, and Lord Nidderdale. Nidderdale flirted with Miss Longestaffe. Marie fell asleep. She secretly told Felix her father was in the book-room below and instructed him to go down and ask to be shown there. She suggested he leave her a note under cover to Madame Didon (Madame Melmotte's personal attendant, called Didon by family). Felix obeyed, descended to book-room where he found Melmotte waking from slumber with cigar in mouth.** **Melmotte immediately assumed Felix came about railway shares and resolved to be stern. Melmotte's strategy: he thrive best by resenting interference in his financier capacity, relying on assumption of superiority to intimidate half-educated men, understanding the game while colleagues did not. With those lacking timidity or ignorance, he cultivated cupidity. He preferred young associates as more timid and less greedy. Lord Nidderdale's suggestions already put to rest; he anticipated no greater difficulty with Felix. Lord Alfred had required purchase.** **Felix wished himself at Beargarden. He had come on business—marriage proposal—but felt unreceived with good humour. When Melmotte asked about his income, Felix considered telling truth (nasty for moment but ending misery by honesty) but lacked courage. Said "It isn't a large property, you know."** **Melmotte, puzzled by English peerage and property descent, questioned how Felix—a baronet and presumed family head—could be heir to Roger Carbury, an Esquire. Felix walking to club afterward felt checkmated and full of wrath at Melmotte's insolence. Recognized game likely over despite believing he could marry Marie (she loved him, was fool, father acknowledged possibility). But Melmotte was no ordinary father—Felix deemed him greatest brute ever created. Remembered Melmotte's elevated eyebrows, brazen forehead, hard mouth. Unable to stand against him, Felix cursed and swore in cab to Beargarden.**

**Sheepstone Meeting (Sunday, 19th April)**: Met Ruby Ruggles beneath tree in grass meadow; spent half hour with her. Made promises and spoke of love with contempt tone; found her appearance common. Promised to see her again Tuesday morning at kitchen garden bottom when grandfather at Harlestone market. Resolved not to keep promise; planned to write asking her to come to London, sending money for journey.

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable; admitted other reasons existed. Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," promising not to see her three months but nothing further. Wore rose from Roger's room on bosom. When met Roger at door, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Understands mother's "tortuous mazes of manoeuvres," disliking them but refraining from rebukes. **Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening), stating constancy; Henrietta has not committed; Roger's determination remains unshaken.**

## Ruby Ruggles
- Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles, of Sheep's Acre, parish of Sheepstone, close to Bungay. Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion; strong, healthy, tall; possessed own will. Had been to marry John Crumb (marriage postponed or abandoned). Understood degradation must be avoided. After Sunday meeting with Felix, resolved: "I suppose I am to be his wedded wife...I'll never be nothing unless I'm that."

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Arrived London from Paris within two years. Claims English birth though speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. In City, his name "worth any money." Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs; has Caversham and old Sussex property. Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary. During Whitsun week country visit, remained in summer-house with Lord Alfred, smoking, drinking brandy and seltzer, appearing not in good humour. Company existed less than six weeks; by Chapter 33 Board day (Friday following Sunday), has twice sold fifty shares at £112 10s., receiving cheques for £625 each representing £25 profit per share above £100 nominal price. Miles Grendall arranged allocation, assuring Felix shares were certain income. Melmotte gracious to Lord Nidderdale; told him to wait, shares allocated but not transferable until he qualifies by investing a few thousand pounds. **Sunday afternoon: Rested in book-room with cigar, generally spending Sunday afternoons there with Lord Alfred, meditating on millions and arranging prices of money for New York, Paris, London Exchanges. Felix's visit immediately suggested to him that baronet came about railway shares; resolved to be stern and perhaps rude, believing he risen high enough to venture such conduct. His strategy: intimidate through assumed superiority, trade on timidity or ignorance of colleagues, or cultivate their cupidity. When neither sufficed, no recourse but purchase (as with Lord Alfred). Young associates preferred as more timid and less greedy. Upon Felix's inquiry about income, Melmotte puzzled by English peerage system—how could baronet (family head) be heir to Esquire? Pressed Felix on property and income questions.**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well as foreigner; has begun forming own opinions. Absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough; has experience with Lord Nidderdale. Currently pursued by Sir Felix Carbury (claimed favourite in London). **Sunday: Fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Contrived to be alone with lover near window for few seconds, telling him "Papa is down-stairs in the book-room. Lord Alfred was told when he came that he was out." Instructed Felix to go down and ask to be shown into book-room. Resolved on constancy toward Felix; rejected other suitors. Felt complete happiness; expressed emotion saying "no one ever did it before." Promised to tell mother though acknowledged "Mamma does not care much about me." Blushes when Felix mentioned, fearing his faithlessness.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Gracious as usual but never very gracious. Called Miss Longestaffe coming "a great bore" and "fatigante." Dismissed Marie's declarations of caring. Appears to know of Felix's offer and does not absolutely disapprove.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no more London expenses that year; family will not return to London from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him. Broke promise to Georgiana of returning to London; refused to argue and ordered her away.

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Strong-minded protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London. Father promised return but now refuses. Felt "treachery"; would not have left town but for that promise. Told father "you have simply and with premeditation broken your word to us." Father refused to argue; she was "partly cowed." Meditated revenge; resolved: "I will do something. I'm not going to be cheated and swindled." Considered writing letter to father. Most angered that family "should have condescended to be civil to the Melmottes down in the country." Wrote letter requesting money to stay with Primeros (Julia Primero's house, Queen's Gate, London) with only her maid; required horse for riding. Following morning, Lady Pomona handed Georgiana undated invitation from Melmotte to stay with them. Breathed very hard; noted insolence. Questioned mother. Expressed contempt for Melmottes, calling them vulgar, beneath apothecary in Bungay. Yet concluded: "I'll go." Did not speak to father that night. Lady Pomona informed Mr. Longestaffe that invitation was to be accepted; Georgiana would go up Friday following. **Friday morning before departure to railway station, conversation between Georgiana and younger sister Sophia was "almost touching." Georgiana failed to hold up her head as usual; task cowed her. Told Sophia: "Sophy, I do so envy you staying here." By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square in drawing-room with Madame Melmotte, Marie, and Lord Nidderdale, carrying on flirtation with Nidderdale in half whisper, wholly indifferent to hostess or young lady of house. Nidderdale said "We know what brings you here."**

**Sophia Longestaffe**: Younger Miss Longestaffe. Somewhat reconciled to country sojourn as it inflicted fitting punishment on Georgiana and because Mr. Whitstable's proximity made difference.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has own rooms in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings.

**Lady Pomona**: Complained of headache at Caversham; slept through afternoon's tension.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Fisker considers cost questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government; correspondence maintained with Mexican President.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

**Fisker's Departure**: Started Saturday morning, 19th April. Met by Nidderdale and Montague.

**Paul Montague**: Junior member of firm. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination. Trembles for his money. Living at Beargarden; entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte in Grosvenor Square. Saw good deal of Sir Felix, Lord Nidderdale; champagne consumption increased. Could not wake up on London mornings with satisfactory thoughts as at Carbury Hall. At Beargarden cardroom, offered to undertake Grendall's debt himself; disallowed.

## Lord Nidderdale
**Intent on marrying Marie Melmotte for her fortune. Discussed moral philosophy with Felix Carbury: invoked Bible passage about forgiving trespasses, distinguishing between various vices. Asked if Felix ever reads Bible. Expressed uncertainty whether he wants to marry Marie if money is not all there. Claims not afraid of Melmotte, believing Melmotte "rather likes me, because I've always been on the square with him," asserting "If it depended on him, you know, I should have the girl to-morrow." On Friday Board day, walked with Melmotte to Abchurch Lane offices, asking about his position regarding shares. Melmotte told him to wait, shares would be allocated but not transferable until he qualifies by investing "a few thousand pounds." Sunday: Present at Grosvenor Square drawing-room, flirting with Miss Longestaffe in half whisper, wholly indifferent to hostess or young lady of house.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase entirely belongs to Bundlesham estate. Firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile." Took degree at Oxford; became "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning day-labourer's wages; forced to buy second-hand clothes. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet condemns himself for harsh words. During Sunday evening with Father Barham, engaged in theological debate; became tired of priest's intolerance. Later showed courtesy as host despite disapproval of Melmotte scheme.

## Father John Barham
Priest of Beccles. Dogmatic Catholic; believes man should abandon reason to care of another or others. Faith sufficient unto itself; moral conduct testimony of faith. At Sunday dinner, discussed Beccles morality with bishop, asserting "his people" more moral though poorer. In county only twelve months; knew nearly every Roman Catholic's name within borders.

## Property Relations
**Daniel Ruggles' Land**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm on bishop's lease, part of property which belonged to bishopric of Elmham. Also holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate; thus one of Roger Carbury's tenants. Sheepstone Birches (wood/copse) belonged to Roger.
